Title: To Solve TBTF Problem, Nudge Shareholders | American Banker
Short-Term Shareholder Thinking Ruins Banks, Krawcheck Says. The respected former B of A executive says shareholder capitalism has gone awry, and that bank directors should be just as worried about outperforming business units as laggard ones. The Absurdity of Too Big to Fail Banking. The supersized bank problem is still alive. Furthermore, these venti-financials continue to grow despite efforts like the Dodd Frank Act. Threatened government breakups of or caps on supersized banks are easier to do in theory than in practice. Shareholder impatience over lagging economic performance is likely to be the catalyst triggering a supersized bank breakup. Furthermore, these giants trade at a 40% discount to their smaller and more focused large regional bank counterparts. Performance issues with their high cost and capital intensive universal banking business model underlie these discounts. The size and complexity of the supersized banks makes them inefficient, hard to manage, difficult to control and rife with conflicts. These factors more than offset the alleged diversification and cross-selling benefits of universal banking. The unspoken Too Big to Fail policy provides an implicit subsidy to these banks by guaranteeing their senior debt. Experts believe the subsidy is worth an estimated $4 to $5 billion per year for each of these trillion dollar plus banks. Supersized institutions are, in effect, the new government-sponsored entities joining Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Consequently, they enjoy an advantage over regional and community banks. Regulators can solve the supersized bank problem by removing barriers to market forces. The requirement should be high enough to encourage the banks to become more focused. Director Thomas Hoenig, this would ensure these banks are too safe to fail without government subsidies. The decline in returns would create a value gap too large to ignore for the supersized banks. Besides divestment or sale, banks can spinoff (usually tax free) existing divisions through a pro rata distribution of subsidiaries shares to existing shareholders. Change is coming to the supersized banks. This will undoubtedly curb the enthusiasm of bank managers to supersize their institutions. results.title: Consensus Is Elusive on TBTF, Big-Bank Subsidies | American Banker
results.content:
Title: Consensus Is Elusive on TBTF, Big-Bank Subsidies | American Banker
WASHINGTON — Banking analysts, former regulators, lawmakers, banking industry representatives and top academics spent more than an hour and a half debating how best to resolve the issue of "too big to fail" on Tuesday, and came away with no easy solutions. Indeed, the conversation, hosted by American Banker and Federal Financial Analytics, covered the gamut, from whether big banks still receive a subsidy for the perception they are "too big to fail," to the exact impact the Brown-Vitter bill would have if enacted into law. While there have been a number of studies by economists undertaken to determine the actual subsidy, or funding advantage, that the largest U.S. financial institutions receive, only one has been cited repeatedly by lawmakers and proponents of a big bank breakup. Saltzman said there should be a study that shows the "positive subsidy" that the largest banks pay through the Deposit Insurance Fund or the Durbin amendment that restricts interchange fees on debit cards. But Simon Johnson, an economist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and co-author of *13 Bankers: The Wall Street Takeover and the Next Financial Meltdown*, disagreed, arguing that out of the roughly two dozen studies available, only one suggested that 'too big to fail' banks didn't receive a subsidy. Greg Baer, a general counsel at JPMorgan Chase, said that banks have also already spent a vast amount of time preparing for how Title II of the Dodd-Frank Act will work in the event of another crisis. Brown and Vitter said that wasn't their intent, saying instead they were targeted on eliminating banks' subsidy for the perception of "too big to fail.". Yet most participants of the forum said the end result of the bill, a draft of which would require megabanks to hold 15% in capital, would result in big banks becoming smaller or breaking themselves up. Wayne Abernathy, executive vice president for financial institutions policy, of the American Bankers Association, said that observers should focus on three parts of bank safety: capital, liquidity, and earnings. But Brown said banks don't necessarily need to curb profits to build capital. "The anger at bankers is being directed at the banks," she said.

results.title: Did Subsidies to Too-Big-To-Fail Banks Increase during the COVID-19 Pandemic? - Liberty Street Economics
results.content: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York works to promote sound and well-functioning financial systems and markets through its provision of industry and payment services, advancement of infrastructure reform in key markets and training and educational support to international institutions. In a recent post, I showed that the implicit funding subsidies to systemically important banks (SIBs) declined, on average, after a set of reforms for eliminating TBTF perceptions was implemented. In this post, I discuss whether these subsidies increased again during the COVID-19 pandemic and, if so, whether the increase accrued to large firms in *all* sectors of the economy. Such concerns, if widely shared, might increase expectations of large bank bailouts and implicit subsidies. As in my previous post, I estimate the implicit subsidy by first constructing a TBTF risk factor, and then estimating exposures to this factor for SIBs and other large financial firms, as detailed in my related study. The TBTF risk factor is based on the idea that the largest financial firms have a higher probability of bailout and so investors perceive them to be less risky and have lower expected equity returns, relative to other large financial firms. In order to estimate the implicit subsidy to SIBs, we consider the exposures of SIBs and other large non-SIB financial firms to the TBTF risk factor. Since SIBs benefit when they are perceived to be TBTF, they should have a lower TBTF risk exposure than non-SIBs. This differential exposure is a measure of the subsidy to SIBs. Our methodology accounts for the *systematic risk* of large banks, or how much their returns co-move with the market return. In the chart below, we show the evolution of the implicit TBTF subsidy for the global portfolio, expressed as a lower equity cost of capital for SIBs relative to three other groups: large non-SIB banks, large nonbank financials, and large nonfinancial firms. Asani Sarkar, “Did Subsidies to Too-Big-To-Fail Banks Increase during the COVID-19 Pandemic?,” Federal Reserve Bank of New York *Liberty Street Economics*, February 11, 2021,. results.title: Tax Breaks are NOT Subsidies
results.content:
Title: Tax Breaks are NOT Subsidies
# Tax Breaks Are NOT Subsidies. Tax Breaks Are NOT SubsidiesLet it be known that I oppose ALL bailouts, bail-ins, subsidies and welfare. I don’t like paying for corporations to stay in business except through the use of their goods and services. Here’s where I get annoyed: it’s still called a subsidy when corporations receive tax breaks. Tax breaks are NOT subsidies. I’ve said this before, but it’s worth mentioning again, when government allows people to keep their money, that is not a cost to the government. Behold: If I claim the interest on my student loans or the interest on my mortgage on my taxes, I get an exemption. It’s not considered “welfare” that I have a reduced tax obligation due to exemptions that I claim. Moreover, the fact that I pay a lower effective tax rate than someone like Mitt Romney is likewise NOT called a subsidy. At no point does anyone say people in lower tax brackets are being subsidized by the government, unless they are actually on the dole. This is why we have a tax code in the United States that makes “War and Peace” look like a trifold. But what is interesting, is they include the all these “tax incentives” which have nothing to do with receiving money from other tax payers. Grants, some bonds, reimbursements are all forms of money coming from the other tax payers. It should be called out separately to show that there are benefits to low/no taxes. There’s $44 Million awarded in actual tax payer money for their infrastructure and training facility. I mean, sure, the citizens of the state of Washington could begrudge the fact that a large corporation like Boeing is dodging nearly $11 Billion in taxes, but if Boeing were to just up and leave the state of Washington, which it has every right to do, and “shop” for a more tax friendly location… then Washington loses the jobs and whatever tax benefits it did get from Boeing altogether. I think it’s fabulous, however, that corporations DO pit government against government to get the best tax rate!
